name: Clark's house at the forks, 1812
aka: 'one near the forks of the river occupied by a man named Clark who was a cattle dealer' (Surgeon Cooper, in Quaife 1913)

documented_range.note: THE RANGE IS INFERRED FROM TWO WITNESSES OF 1808 AND A BOUND THIS PROJECT CHOSE. It opens on 25 January 1808, the date Whistler's draught carries, the one day a source shows the house standing; Surgeon Cooper, at the post from 1808, counts 'one near the forks of the river occupied by a man named Clark who was a cattle dealer' (Quaife 1913 p. 167). It may be older. No source read for T-2512 mentions it after Cooper's years, so its standing on the scene date of August 1812 is inferred from continuity, as the La Lime house's is. It is closed on 3 July 1816, the day before the troops came back to rebuild the fort: nothing read names a house at the forks in any account of the reoccupied post, and the close keeps it out of every scene after 1812 rather than carrying an unwitnessed house into one. The close is reconstructed (L-1812-forks-2512).

position.symbolic_location: On the south bank of the main river at the forks, east of the South Branch, beside the west end of the company cornfield (forks_company_cornfield_1812). Local E +127.6..+132.3, N -92.4..-87.5.
position.note: Whistler's draught of 25 January 1808 draws two small houses at the bottom left of the sheet, where the double line of the river (index no. 25) meets a second double line lettered 'One branch of Cheykago River': one in the angle between the branch and the river, across the river from the fort, and one on the fort's side of the river beside the dotted outline lettered 'Company Garden & public Cornfield Eight acres'. Quaife (1913 p. 167): 'Whistler's drawing represents two houses at the forks, one occupied by a discharged soldier.' The committed trace's 34-item index does not number them; they were found on the pinned sheet at T-2512. THE RULING: this is the house drawn on the fort's side of the river, beside the cornfield's lettering, so it stands on the south bank of the main stem east of the South Branch, which is where Quaife's 'close to the forks on the south side of the main river' puts the cornfield. On the committed forks water (Wright 1834, +/-20 m) it is seated about 45 m south of the main stem's south bank and 70 m east of the South Branch's east bank, and about 20 m west of the cornfield's fence. The sheet's distances here are not to any scale, so nothing nearer is claimed. Rotation 0 is a reconstruction (L-1812-forks-2512).

derivation.reason: Not by any of validate.py's methods (platted corner, traced waterline, street frontage). The draught says its outside buildings are 'not laid down by a scale' and the forks lie far beyond any part T-2062's arrangement rule can open out, so the seat is a stated ruling on the committed forks water (data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/river.geojson, carried into the 1812 field), recorded as L-1812-forks-2512.

footprint.note: THE DRAWN BOX AT THE INDEX'S FORTY FEET TO THE INCH, the scale the draught states for the Indian Department's dwellings and the one T-2062 reads every outside building at: sheet px [502, 1877, 537, 1913] (about +/-5 px) at 90.4 px to the inch is 15.5 x 15.9 ft. The drawing is a small pictorial elevation, roof and front together, so this is an upper bound (L-1812-forks-2512).

stories.note: Unattested. The draught draws a one-storey house; one storey with the roof space over it.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. About eight feet of log to the plate.

construction.note: No source states the material. Log is the bounded reading: every house at the post before 1812 whose material the histories give is log, and Quaife calls the factor's and the agent's houses 'two log houses' (L-1812-forks-2512).

roof_type.note: The draught draws a pitched roof over the house, as it does for the agent's house and the factory; a gable is the reading this project takes for all of them.

roof_pitch_deg.note: Unattested; no source describes the roof.

chimneys.note: Unattested. One end chimney, the least a winter house needs; no source places it.

phases.change_note: Built T-2512 (2026-10-15), one of the two houses Whistler's 1808 draught draws at the forks of the river, in the 1812 scene.

function.note: A dwelling. Cooper: 'occupied by a man named Clark who was a cattle dealer' (Quaife 1913 p. 167). That Clark's house is this drawn one is a reconstruction (L-1812-forks-2512).

research_note: CLARK'S HOUSE AT THE FORKS (T-2512). Surgeon Cooper, at Fort Dearborn from 1808, remembered 'one near the forks of the river occupied by a man named Clark who was a cattle dealer' (Quaife 1913 p. 167); nothing else read gives Clark a first name or a date. WHICH HOUSE IS WHOSE IS NOT READ. Cooper, at the post from 1808, counts 'one near the forks of the river occupied by a man named Clark who was a cattle dealer' (Quaife 1913 p. 167); Whistler, the same winter, draws two at the forks and Quaife says one was a discharged soldier's. THE RULING: Clark's is the other of Whistler's two, so the forks have two houses and not three. Cooper's count of the houses round the post names one at the forks where Whistler draws two, and nothing read puts a third there; merging the cattle dealer into the draught's second house is the reading that adds no house a source does not draw. Which of the two drawn houses was Clark's and which the soldier's is not on the sheet as read: the lettering beside the western house is legible only as '... by the man of the House'. So this one, on the fort's side of the river beside the garrison's cornfield, is given to Clark and the north-bank house to the soldier, and the choice is reconstructed. Everything of its shape is the archetype's small log house at the draught's drawn size (an upper bound); its seat is a ruling on the committed forks water. Nobody is drawn in or near it (L1).
